data.title: Full-Stack Developer at AxiomQ
data.subtitle: August 2026 – Present
data.excerpt: Where I am now, and the first job where I work on both ends of the stack. So far that has meant two projects: an events platform for a large pharmaceutical company and an application that extends a cloud-based ERP. Neither client can be named, so there are no screenshots.

sections.label: Two projects
sections.title: An events platform and an ERP sync engine
sections.lede: Both live in monorepos with NestJS on the server and React or Next.js in the browser, and on both I write code on each side.

items.name: Events platform
items.summary: A platform for running large professional events and the content shared around them.

built.body: Connections to the client's internal systems, its SDKs and outside data sources. Events between services go through a transactional outbox, so an event only leaves once the change behind it is committed.
Modular scheduling, with integrations into third-party calendars.
I helped build the in-house React component library the product's screens are made from.

items.name: ERP extension
items.summary: An application that adds custom business features on top of a cloud-based ERP, so its users can do that work in one place.

built.body: A sync engine I designed and built. It keeps data consistent between the application and the ERP in near real time, in both directions, on custom job queues and sync workers.
The ERP's API and webhooks wired into the application, with custom modules built on top of them.

data.title: Front-end Developer at NQode
data.subtitle: April 2024 – June 2026
data.excerpt: An agency in Novi Sad, and three clients through it: full-stack work on a greenhouse platform, sixteen months as the only front-end developer on a prop trading app, then marketing sites with a lot of motion for a digital agency.

highlights: SSR and SEO at Source AG

index.note: Full-stack: server rendering, SEO, deploys and tests

index.label: BrightFunded
index.note: The only front-end developer, for sixteen months

sections.label: Source AG
sections.title: Moving a greenhouse platform's rendering to the server
sections.lede: Source makes AI tools for commercial greenhouse growers. I worked across the stack there, on Next.js and Nest.js.
body: The main job was moving rendering out of the browser. Pages arrived from the server already built, for a faster first load and markup search engines could crawl. Around that I set up the SEO, the deploy pipeline and the tests.

shot.caption: Source · public site
shot.alt: Source's public home page: AI solutions for smarter greenhouse cultivation, with photos of tomatoes on the vine

built.body: A Next.js application rendered on the server, with Nest.js behind it.
Meta tags, structured data and server-rendered markup, so the content can be indexed.
GraphQL and REST APIs feeding the interface.
Vercel CI/CD that ships serverless functions on every merge to main.
Playwright end-to-end tests on the critical user journeys, and Jest for unit tests.

sections.label: BrightFunded
sections.title: The only front-end developer on a prop trading app
sections.lede: BrightFunded is a prop trading firm that funds traders. For sixteen months I was the only front-end developer on its client app, and the UI was mine from end to end.
body: The app has about twelve screens, all built and maintained by me. The hardest was the purchase flow, which is heavily customised. Because nobody else worked on the front end, the structure, the tests and the rules for working on it were mine to set up too.

shot.caption: BrightFunded · public site
shot.alt: BrightFunded's public home page on a dark background: 'We fund traders up to 400K' above a Get Funded button and a row of trader payouts

built.body: A modular Angular and TypeScript structure, laid out so new features could be added without reworking the ones already there.
Around 35 components under every screen, which kept the interface consistent and made new screens quicker to build.
There were none when I started. I added Playwright and brought coverage of the critical flows above 60%.
Linting rules, a code review process and onboarding docs, so the next developer would not start from nothing.

sections.label: Owow
sections.title: Marketing sites with a lot of motion
sections.lede: Owow is a digital agency. My last stretch at NQode went to their marketing sites, built together with their designers.
body: The sites are animation-heavy, with the motion written in GSAP. Content is managed in Payload CMS and rendered by Next.js, with Tailwind for the styling.

shot.caption: Owow · public site
shot.alt: Owow's own site on black: selected work shown as large device mockups with project names and service tags

built.body: A Next.js front end that reads its content from Payload CMS. I built it and then kept it running.
Responsive layouts in Tailwind, kept close to the Figma designs.
Regular back-and-forth with the designers, so what shipped matched what they drew and the components stayed consistent from page to page.

sections.label: In-house
sections.title: A component library for NQode itself
sections.lede: Besides the client work, I built the component library under the internal tools NQode makes for its own use.

data.title: Front-end Developer at EPAM Systems
data.subtitle: February 2022 – April 2024
data.excerpt: Two years on one live product: Meridianbet, a sports betting and casino site in more than 50 markets. I built betting features in Angular, standalone apps in React, the visuals for three casino games and admin tools for the client's executives.

sections.label: The product
sections.title: A betting site that stayed live while we shipped into it
sections.meta: Meridianbet · Sports betting and casino · 50+ markets
sections.lede: Meridianbet was my only client at EPAM. Its sports betting and casino product runs in more than 50 markets, and it stayed live the whole time we were shipping into it.
body: Most of my days went into the main Angular app. Alongside it I built smaller standalone apps in React, and the internal admin tools the client's executives used to manage users and read reports.

shot.caption: Meridianbet · home with live odds
shot.alt: Meridianbet's home page: casino promotions across the top, featured matches with odds, a live football table, and the bet slip on the right

built.body: Interactive features in the Angular app, along with the everyday fixes that kept it moving.
Smaller apps built in React, separate from the main Angular codebase.
Internal tools for user management and reporting, used by the client's executive team.

sections.label: The games
sections.title: Three casino games, from a Blender scene to a live bet
sections.meta: Visuals · Animation · Game logic · Real-time data
sections.lede: I owned the front-end visuals for three of the site's casino games: the art, the animation, the game logic in the browser, and the link to the game engine on the server.
body: I made the assets in Blender and turned them into frame-by-frame CSS sprite animations. The game logic ran in plain JavaScript. Angular handled the ticket and bet data, and WebSockets carried real-time betting updates between the game and a C++ engine on the back end.

sections.title: A 25-person team with strict QA
body: Designers handed us specs, product owners brought the business requirements, and the engineers turned both into shipped features. Seven QA engineers checked everything by hand and with automation. The checks were strict and the deadlines were tight.

data.title: Front-end Developer at Codeplicity
data.subtitle: February 2021 – February 2022
data.excerpt: My first job: a seven-person agency in Novi Sad. I wrote reusable JavaScript components and modular Sass for client sites built on PHP templates, and learned the work in code reviews and pair programming with the senior developers.

sections.label: First job
sections.title: Client sites on PHP templates, with a small team
sections.lede: Everyone worked in one office, designers and back-end developers included. Client sites rendered on PHP, and my JavaScript and Sass went into those templates.
body: Projects ran locally in Vagrant boxes that someone else set up. I worked next to the senior developers through code reviews and pair programming, and saw client sites through from design to launch with them.

built.body: UI components in plain JavaScript, written to be carried from one client site to the next.
Styles organised as a modular Sass architecture.
Older front-end code on client projects, refactored and brought up to date.
